title: Dragons' Den IP Blog - Series 23 Episode 8

content.content: It’s the return of series 23 of Dragons' Den and tonight's episode served up plenty of food for thought, with confectionery creativity and spice-inspired stories firmly on the menu.

Hitting the sweet spot were John and Sean, founders of Mr Swainston's Traditional Sweet Emporium. Inspired by Beamish Museum's authentic old-fashioned sweet shop, the self-proclaimed 'Ant & Dec of the sweet shop world' turned nostalgia into a thriving business. After building a loyal TikTok following and opening their first shop in South Shields, they entered the Den hoping to take their sweet empire beyond the North East.
Looking every part the wartime sweet shop owners, right up to their flat caps, the pair brought their ‘travelling sweet shop’ into the Den in search of a £50,000 investment for 10% of the business.

While impressed by the pair's passion and growing following, the Dragons questioned what would set the business apart in a crowded confectionery market. Susie Ma's suggestion that John and Sean could find their flavour by developing their own range of sweets was echoed by Peter Jones and Deborah Meaden.
Secrets of the trade

If John and Paul create a sweet that's good enough to rival Willy Wonka's Everlasting Gobstopper, keeping the recipe under wraps could be just as important as creating it. Wonka's battles with confectionery copycats weren't entirely make-believe, drawing inspiration from real-life confectionery espionage, where rivals sought to uncover closely guarded creations and manufacturing methods.

These days, trade secrets can help businesses protect the recipes, processes and special ingredients that make their products unique. Rather than being registered, they rely on businesses keeping valuable information under wraps through measures such as restricted access and non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).
You can find several example NDAs on our website, though it's always wise to have a legal professional draw up an NDA that meets your specific needs.
The famously secret Irn-Bru formula is a perfect example of commercial secrecy preserving a product's distinctive appeal. Read our Irn Bru case study to find out more.

Jenna Meek was the only Dragon to bite, drawing on her own experience of building a global brand from small beginnings. She offered £50,000 and her branding expertise for 20% of the business, reducing to 12% once she'd recouped her investment. It was a sweet deal for both sides, with John and Sean accepting the offer and leaving the Den with an investment.
A family affair

No sooner had the sugar rush settled, Spice Kitchen arrived to spice things up. Mother-and-son duo Shashi and Sanjay, founders of Spice Kitchen, entered the Den seeking £75,000 for 5% of their business.

Inspired by Shashi's deep-rooted expertise, family recipes and culinary influences gathered through years of travel, Spice Kitchen creates high-quality spice blends and beautifully crafted spice tins wrapped in hand-stitched upcycled sari fabric.

Their products are already stocked by hundreds of high-end retailers across the UK, and the pair have also taken steps to protect the brand they've  carefully cultivated, securing a registered trade mark for Spice Kitchen.

Building a successful business is one thing, building a recognisable brand is another. A registered trade mark helps protect brand identity, giving the owner exclusive rights to use them for the goods and services covered by the registration and helping distinguish them from competitors.
The Dragons were treated to a flavour-packed sample of their homemade samosas and signature spice blends, hoping the flavours would prove as irresistible as the business itself.
While the Dragons were impressed by the business, they questioned how Spice Kitchen could continue to differentiate itself.

As the conversation continued, it became clear that Spice Kitchen was about far more than sales figures. When Susie asked Shashi what the business meant to her, Shashi explained that she wanted to pass on her knowledge and share it with others rather than take it with her.
It was a sentiment that resonated around the Den. One by one, the Dragons decided not to invest - not because they doubted the business, but because they admired it.

In a rare show of agreement, the Dragons encouraged Shashi and Sanjay to take pride in what they had already created. As Peter Jones put it, bringing in outside investment at this stage could do more harm than good.
Sometimes the best recipe doesn't need any extra ingredients.
If you have a business idea and would like to find out more about how IP can protect it, visit our free online step by step IP guidance, that can help.

title: Tackling drought: aquifer recharging to smart irrigation trials

content.content: As summers grow drier and water levels fall, farmers face an increasing challenge in meeting the water needs of crops and livestock.
Without solutions, this puts yields, and ultimately businesses, at risk.
A package of drought support for farmers was recently announced by the Prime Minister, including:
In addition to these measures, one way we're supporting farms is through investment in innovation.

Through the Farming Innovation Programme and its ADOPT Fund (Accelerating Development of Practices and Technologies), we’re backing farmer-led ideas that strengthen access to water and help businesses adapt to increasingly hot and dry weather.
In this post, we share 3 farmer-led projects already underway.
Aquifer recharging: banking winter rainfall for summer droughts
In East Anglia, it is harder for growers of crops like potatoes and vegetables to secure reliable water supplies for irrigation.
Summer river abstraction is becoming harder, and reservoirs are a large investment.
You can find out more on funding that the government is providing for the construction of on-farm reservoirs later in this post.
Meanwhile, an ADOPT-funded project is testing whether a solution lies underground.
William Kerr Farms in Suffolk is testing a reliable alternative to reservoirs called Managed Aquifer Recharge.

Underground aquifers are usually filled very slowly through rainfall. This project speeds that up, pumping in water from rivers in the winter during the wet season, storing water when it is plentiful.
This technique has been used across the world in drier climates, but is rare in the UK.
The project is testing the construction and use of an artificial aquifer, looking at the commercial viability for farms in England.
With England’s unique geological conditions, the project is testing how quickly water can be extracted during summer when crop demand is at its peak.
As well as being more economical to build than reservoirs, less water is lost through evaporation. By sitting below the crops, it also doesn't use up farmland.
This trial aims to demonstrate that the technology can work in England. If successful, this could be rolled out more widely across the country.
Smart irrigation: precision watering to tackle a gap in yield
Conventional hose-reel irrigation applies water evenly, despite differences in soil drainage across a field.
Heavier soils may be over-watered while sandier patches receive too little water. Research suggests that this imbalance leads to yield losses of 10-20%.
This is a common challenge for growers. An ADOPT-funded project is focused on precise irrigation to improve productivity with less water.

The trial with Waldersey Farms in Cambridgeshire and Elveden Estate in Suffolk, working with Water Resources East, is developing a smart irrigation system for onions and potatoes, aiming to improve crop yield while cutting costs.
Over 2 growing seasons, the team behind the project are comparing both conventional and advanced irrigation systems to track yield, quality of product, and costs on different soil types.
The advanced irrigation system uses data on soil, crop growth, and weather to apply the optimal amount of water to each 20 x 20 metre piece of land.
Previous evidence suggests the approach could deliver water and energy savings of 20-25%, along with yield gains.
The trial is testing whether those benefits hold up under everyday conditions.
Floatovoltaics: turning farm reservoirs into income-generating assets

Farm reservoirs give farmers a resilient water supply. We are taking steps to ensure farmers have the confidence to invest in reservoirs to guarantee water supplies during the growing season by storing water captured over the winter months. There is a way they could generate income for farm businesses too.

Funding secured through the 2023 Farming Futures competition has enabled Cranfield University and Pollybell Farm, a broccoli, cauliflower and cabbage producer near Doncaster, to explore how floating solar panels, known as floatovoltaics, can generate an additional source of farm income.
These floating panels work like ground-mounted solar panels, but free up farmland. They also shade the water from evaporation losses and run more efficiently from the natural water cooling.
The project team is using wireless sensor data to conduct research on farm. It has collated 2 years of real data from the solar panels, reservoir water and the farm's energy use.
Farmer James Brown explained that installing floating panels was an obvious way forward to increase farm generation of renewable energy and to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels.
The project team has since produced a practical guide to help other farmers considering the technology for their own reservoirs.
The guide covers planning permission, anchoring systems, maintenance and the financial benefits of investing in floating solar. Visit the UK Irrigation Association website for updates.
Apply for ADOPT funding
Two of the projects featured in this post received support through ADOPT. If you have an idea you'd like to test on your farm, applications are now open.
We blogged about the current opportunities today, but you can also find out more about ADOPT and the official grant guidance on the UKRI website.
New grant for building on-farm reservoirs
As mentioned, for farmers looking to build new on-farm reservoirs, a new £15 million Water Management Grant will be available from this autumn.
This complements wider government action to make it easier to secure planning permission for this kind of infrastructure.
We'll publish further information when the grant guidance and application details are available.

title: A Digital Fast Stream Secondments Journey: How the secondment strengthened my product and strategy Skills

content.content: Hi, I’m Marjanul Islam. As I write this, I am currently in my second year on the Digital Fast Stream working as a Delivery Manager.

As part of the programme, I completed a six-month secondment outside government. In this blog, I reflect on the work, challenges, and lessons learned from my secondment in a commercial environment outside government, and how it boosted my confidence and skills.

The Fast Stream Secondment is an optional or scheme-dependent placement where participants form Fast Stream step out of central government, typically for 6 months to work in an external host organisation. Secondments expose civil servants to lean budgets, direct operational delivery, and different organisational cultures outside government. Fast Streamers tackle strategic, high-value projects for host organisations while bringing back commercial, non-profit, or media insights to policy making.
Why did you choose to do a secondment?
My motivation for this secondment was to experience a different working environment.
My background before the Fast Stream included time in an MP's office, followed by a policy role at the Department for Business and Trade.
The secondment was invaluable, allowing me to gain experience outside the Civil Service and bring back important lessons, all without having to leave my career here permanently.

My secondment as a Product Manager was with the Commercial team which focused on generating reinvestment income. The Product team was new, so my role involved significant market research, identifying opportunities, and launching new products to test market viability.
What surprised you about the secondment?
I expected my six-month at the placement to be largely observational, not anticipating mostly learning as an external joiner.
However, the role was surprisingly hands-on, significantly challenging and stretching me, and ultimately boosting my confidence.
What did your secondment involve?
I was acting as the lead Product Manager for an external client’s product.

The product aimed to help organisations use their data to make better strategic decisions. At the start, the product faced several challenges. It had no active users, limited evidence as to whether it was solving a real problem, and unclear use cases.

The team had just seven weeks to strengthen its position. This meant defining the problem more clearly, identifying priority use cases, and suggesting AI-driven features that users would find useful, and help the product stand out.
For the first two weeks, I focused on building the foundations. I reviewed existing research, created a user research plan interview guide, and the team began recruiting participants for interviews.
The interviews had two main purposes: to understand the challenges organisations face when using their data to make strategic decisions, and to gather feedback on the product.
The aim was to complete five to seven interviews, but recruitment delays quickly became a concern.

I adjusted the plan and brought the secondary research forward so the team could make progress while recruitment continued. Although the secondary research had its limitations, it still gave everyone useful context and prevented the project from losing momentum.
Ultimately, the decision was correct; the interviews yielded the most valuable insights, and early planning and adaptation helped to maintain progress.
What were some valuable learnings or highlights?

Conducting the interviews was a valuable learning experience. I improved how I asked questions and sought guidance after reviewing and reflecting on the first session. By week four, I had successfully interviewed six diverse stakeholders.

The analysis also reinforced the need to use AI carefully. Reviewing the recordings revealed minor errors in the AI-assisted analysis, reinforcing that while AI can support the process, unchecked use can introduce mistakes.

In the final weeks, I worked with the team to produce a detailed report, including strategic recommendations and a product roadmap. This was my first experience having real ownership of decisions that shaped a product’s direction. It was exciting but also challenging. The role pushed me outside my comfort zone and showed me that I can operate confidently at this level.

During the secondment, I also carried out competitor analysis for two products. I reviewed existing analysis, carried out new research, and spoke with colleagues in product, sales, and delivery to review findings.

I then shared the key insights with the team, to help support future decisions. I enjoyed this work because it combined structured research with close collaboration, and showed the value of clear, evidence-based competitor insight.
Would you recommend a secondment?

Looking back, the digital fast stream secondment exceeded my expectations. I learned a great deal about product management, strategy, stakeholder engagement, and working in a commercial environment. This was my first real insight into working outside government

I would recommend a secondment especially for those with limited non-government experience. It offers a chance to develop a well-rounded skillset and try something new without leaving the Civil Service. Since secondments are only six months, be proactive and engage quickly to maximise the opportunity.
Find out more about the Digital and Cyber Fast Stream in this blog

title: How digital verification services can help businesses meet their obligations under the Money Laundering Regulations

content.content: In early 2026 we (DCMS, formerly DSIT) worked with HM Treasury to publish guidance under the Money Laundering Regulations (MLRs). The guidance sets out how certified and registered digital verification services (DVS) that operate in compliance with the UK DVS trust framework (“trust framework”) can be treated as reliable and independent sources of identity verification for MLR-regulated businesses when they need to check customer identities to meet their legal duties , as part of their customer due diligence processes.
We’ve been asked a range of questions about how this new guidance applies to different kinds of DVS. To respond to those questions, this blog post explains:
Identity checks must align to GPG 45 “level of confidence”

Certified and registered DVS must provide an identity check that meets a “level of confidence” as set out in Good Practice Guide 45 (GPG 45). This might be low, medium, high or very high and it indicates how sure the DVS is that the customer is who they say they are. Certified and registered DVS must express identity verification outcomes using GPG 45 levels of confidence because this is required by the trust framework.

Regulated businesses must do a risk assessment when dealing with each of their customers and select the level of assurance that is commensurate with the risks identified. This ensures businesses that are subject to the MLRs decide what level of confidence is right for each customer.

This may affect many existing services that MLR-regulated businesses currently use. It’s important for DVS providers that want to be compliant with the guidance to understand how to avoid producing identity checks that fall short of a GPG 45 level of confidence.

DVS providers seeking certification must ensure their identity verification processes meet the requirements of GPG 45 and the trust framework. Identity outcomes and other attribute data must be handled separately. Separating identity verification from other checks can help providers clearly demonstrate the level of confidence achieved by their identity process, while continuing to offer additional information that supports other business needs.
DVS can provide additional data alongside a level of confidence

Alongside the GPG 45 identity check, a DVS check may return extra data. This could include things like address information or whether the individual is a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) or a sanctions target. We call these pieces of information “attributes”, and they may be useful to meet other business needs.

Where a DVS provides both identity and attribute information, it must clearly distinguish the GPG 45 identity check outcome from the attributes. The MLRs guidance relates specifically to the use of certified and registered DVS for identity verification. As a result, only the identity verification outcome needs to meet GPG 45 requirements. Attributes are not part of the identity check itself and are not covered by the MLRs guidance.

DVS that share attributes must be certified as attribute service providers (ASPs), which means they have been assessed against the attributes guidance. This includes binding attributes to an identity before they are shared.
If a certified ASP does not create, store or share attributes in line with the attributes guidance, it is not compliant with the trust framework requirements.

If a DVS is certified as an identity service provider (IDSP) but not an ASP, the attributes it creates and shares as part of a GPG 45-compliant identity check fall within its certified IDSP service. However, any other attributes it creates or shares fall outside the scope of its IDSP certification and are not covered by the attributes guidance.

DVS must ensure it clearly communicates to relying parties about which attributes form part of its certified service and which do not. Failure to provide this transparency may result in the loss of certification and registration.
Only certified and registered DVS can be relied upon under the MLRs guidance for identity verification

Speciﬁcally, for customers who are individuals, entities can fulﬁl their obligations under Regulation 28 of the Money Laundering Regulations by verifying a customer’s identity using certiﬁed and registered DVS.
There is no obligation to source attributes from certified and registered DVS but it is strongly recommended.

Being listed on the DVS register is the clearest signal that a DVS provider delivers services that are reliable and independently assured against the trust framework, including any attribute services they are certified for. Over time, we expect the quality gap between certified and non-certified providers to matter more for relying parties such as MLR-regulated businesses.
What we’ll do next

We will continue to work with HM Treasury, sector guidance bodies and industry to keep the guidance clear and practical. As implementation progresses, we will use the OfDIA blog to share further guidance and respond to common questions.

title: Preventative Analytics for Youth Justice: The Advisory Panel's First Steps

content.content: Preventing children and young people from being drawn into crime and the criminal justice system can have profound effects later in life. Did you know that 80% of prolific adult offenders get their first cautions or convictions as children? Spotting early vulnerabilities and offering the right support should significantly benefit society, victims, and children and young people themselves.

As the youth justice White Paper makes clear, technology and data might help practitioners across services decide how help should best be offered. A natural starting point for this is enabling easier data sharing between frontline workers like youth justice workers, social workers, teachers and police. Establishing these data flows could also enable machine learning and advanced analytics. Exploring such possibilities, though needs careful safeguarding against bias and criminalisation risks.
Supporting responsible innovation in Youth Justice

The Preventative Analytics for Youth Justice Advisory Panel (PAYJAP) was established in early 2026 to offer one such safeguard. Chaired by Minister Jake Richards, and comprising youth justice academics, practitioners and technologists, it held its first meeting in late June. As this summary of its initial advice shows, the discussion focused heavily on the ethical implications and likely value of preventative analytics. The meeting was held under the Chatham House Rule.
Emerging themes from the panel discussion
Prevention requires a whole-system approach

Panel members emphasised that prevention is a systemic, multi-agency issue, with a range of services (e.g. education, social care and health) all needing to play a role. Within this context, there was also acknowledgement that there is an issue with fragmented data and disconnected systems. Resolving this can help practitioners identify individual children’s unique needs before they reach the attention of the justice system.
Choosing the right terminology is crucial

There was a strong emphasis on choosing the right language and ensuring that it coheres with the Child First approach. Panel members raised concerns that framing children through the lenses of ‘risk’ and ‘prevention’ within a youth justice context is inherently negative. It can contribute criminalisation; it might be exacerbated if vulnerabilities and structural inequalities are interpreted as ‘risk factors’ rather than indicators of unmet need. Participants stressed focusing on a child’s ‘needs’ and ‘strengths'.
Input data should be carefully scrutinised

Children and young people change quickly in a short space of time, especially between ages 11 and 15, one person pointed out. Therefore, it would be risky to assume that trends observed in data at an earlier age will simply continue as a child develops.

Extending this theme, any input data should be rigorously scrutinised to understand its quality and identify any hidden biases, as highlighted by panel members. A participatory approach to design, involving case workers, children and families in developing new analytical methods, could help address these issues.
Outputs must be explainable

Model outputs should be explainable to children, families and practitioners, panel members said. Patterns found by machine learning algorithms might be hard for humans to understand. Starting with a simple approach before trying more complex things would help with transparency and explainability.

And, even if an analytical model could identify concerns about a child, this doesn’t automatically mean that the capacity is in place to act on those concerns, some panel members reflected. MoJ should be sure that the right resources are present, they said.
Tangible examples can help with these dilemmas
Finally, a panel member recommended facing these questions while working through practical examples; these might even be coproduced with communities themselves.
Looking forward

The Minister and the Ministry of Justice will reflect on the advice and recommendations shared by the panel and consider how this has affected ongoing research. An update will be provided at the next PAYJAP meeting which will take place in autumn 2026.
We look forward to future discussions and building on this initial panel meeting.

title: A thinking partner: Copilot as assistive technology

content.content: Since 2023, Defra has been running targeted trials and rollouts of Microsoft Copilot - a personal AI assistant integrated within Microsoft apps. These pilots highlighted the meaningful ways it can benefit colleagues who are neurodivergent and/or have a disability or other access need and, as such, we made full licenses available as a reasonable adjustment. In this blog, Ray Ede from the livestock information transformation programme explains how it supports him day-to-day.

I’ve just started as a delivery manager on the livestock information transformation programme. This, alongside previous roles and apprenticeship studies, involves bringing together complex information, shaping it into something useful, and helping people make sense of it. That can mean drafting documents, reviewing feedback, preparing briefings, and turning messy thinking into something structured and clear.

I’m also neurodivergent, and I process information in my own way. I can need more time to absorb verbal information, hold ideas in mind, and turn them into something I can confidently share. With clear structure, written information, and a little extra time, I can do my best work.

This is where Copilot comes in. I first used the full license as a form of assistive technology during a departmental trial and now use it regularly across Word, Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft 365 applications.

For me, Copilot is much more than a productivity tool; it reduces cognitive load by holding and organising all the moving parts otherwise in my head. This eases a lot of the friction that can sit between having ideas and translating them into a usable form. It’s a practical tool that reduces some of the invisible barriers I experience day-to-day.
Bearing the load

Copilot does not remove the need for thinking. If anything, it gives me more time to think by allowing me to direct my energy away from formatting, sequencing or getting the first draft down, and towards more important work. It helps by first giving me a structure.

For example, I can ask it to turn rough notes into a draft outline, summarise a long document, pull out key actions from a meeting or help me test whether a message is clear. I still review everything, check the facts and decide what to use, but it reduces the cognitive load at the start of the task. That means I can spend more of my effort on judgement, quality and context, rather than wrestling with the blank page.
One of the biggest benefits for me is in writing. I often know what I want to say, but the first version can come out too long, too detailed or not quite in the right order.

Copilot helps me reshape that material into something more readable. I use it to make drafts clearer, shorten text, improve flow and adapt tone depending on whether I am writing a formal document, a Teams update, a briefing or an email. That support helps me communicate with more confidence.

Copilot also supports my memory and organisation. When work involves meetings, long threads, multiple versions of documents and lots of small actions, it is easy for important points to get buried. Being able to ask Copilot to summarise a thread, identify key points or help me produce a cleaner version of an output makes work feel more manageable. It gives me a way back into the detail without having to reread everything from scratch.

Copilot has helped me be more reflective. I have used it to test whether my writing is clear, whether my recommendations are practical and whether I may be over-emphasising one perspective. In that sense, it can act a bit like a thinking partner. Not a decision maker and not a substitute for people, but a useful prompt that helps me pause, check and improve.
My Copilot top tip

My advice to anyone new to Copilot is simple: start small. You do not need the perfect prompt. Like any tool, the more you use it, the more value you discover. Through this experimentation I have learnt to produce prompts that prioritise clarity. I get better results when I explain the audience, the purpose, the tone and the format I want.

For example, I might ask for something to be made more concise, written in plain language, turned into clear bullet points or softened so it sounds more conversational. Those small instructions make a big difference.

Copilot has not changed who I am or how I think. What it has done is given me a more supportive way to work with how I think. It helps me turn complexity into structure, ideas into words, and long tasks into manageable steps. It achieves exactly what assistive technology should: to not make everyone work in the same way but to adapt to individual needs to help people work at their best.

title: Apply now for the latest ADOPT funding rounds

content.content: Eligible applicants can now apply for funding through the latest rounds of the Accelerating Development of Practices and Technologies (ADOPT) Fund.
We know that trying something new on farm can involve time, cost and uncertainty.
ADOPT helps reduce that risk by funding practical, farmer-led on-farm trials and demonstrations that can be tested in real farming conditions and shared more widely.
It focuses on projects that build confidence in new ways of working, helping farmers improve productivity, resilience and sustainability.
Full ADOPT Grant

This grant is designed to support innovative, on-farm trials or experiments to test ideas or solutions and demonstrate that they will address major on-farm or immediate post-farmgate challenges or opportunities.

To support larger and more ambitious projects, we increased the maximum project size from the previous £100,000 to £200,000. As a result, your project’s total costs must be between £50,000 and £200,000.
You can apply now. The deadline to apply is Wednesday 7 October 2026 at 11am.
Read the guidance and apply for the Full ADOPT Grant.
The grant is now in its 9th round.
ADOPT Facilitator Support Grant
This grant provides a £2,500 grant for a farmer, grower or forester based in England to engage an external Project Facilitator to support with submissions into the Full ADOPT Grant competitions.

Project Facilitators can help applicants develop project ideas, shape proposals, build partnerships and identify the expertise needed to support a project.  You can apply now. The deadline to apply is Wednesday 30 September 2026 at 11am. Read the guidance and apply for the Facilitator Support Grant.
The grant is now in its 11th round.
Application support
ADOPT Support Hub
The ADOPT Support Hub, delivered by ADAS, UK Agri-Tech Centre and the Soil Association, can provide support with your application.
It can help you plan your project scope and connect you with relevant technical and industry expertise.
It also supports knowledge sharing between projects across the programme.
ADOPT facilitators
You can also get support from an ADOPT project facilitator, who can help manage your project, prepare reporting documents and keep delivery and communications on track.
The project facilitator directory can help you find someone with relevant regional and sector experience.
Watch the webinar
When the fund launched, Innovate UK delivered a webinar covering the application process.
Listen to the podcast
If you'd like to hear how farmers are accessing ADOPT funding and trialling ideas on their farms, you can listen to our Defra Farming podcast.
In this episode, Thomas Slattery from the Support Hub speaks to Bryony Graham in Essex and Peter Southwell in East Yorkshire.
Case study: Testing tools to improve fertiliser use
Fertiliser is one of the biggest costs for arable farms. Applying too little can reduce yields, while applying too much adds unnecessary costs.
Through ADOPT, farmers in Yorkshire have set up the Yorkshire Crop Nutrition Club to test whether new technologies can help improve fertiliser decisions on farm.

The group is trialling a range of soil sensors, crop monitoring tools and digital technologies across their farms over two growing seasons. By testing these tools in real farming conditions, they aim to find out which approaches provide practical and reliable information that farmers can use.
The farmers will share their findings openly through farmer meetings and peer-to-peer learning. This will help other farmers identify what works and what offers value for money.

Improving nutrient management can help reduce input costs and support more productive farming businesses. It can also help lower environmental impacts, as nitrogen fertiliser contributes significantly to the carbon footprint of many arable crops, including wheat.
By improving the accuracy of fertiliser applications, the group hopes to support both farm profitability and long-term sustainability.

title: The Secret Life of a Suburban Garden Visitor

content.content: As dusk settles over the gardens on my terrace row, most of us are drawing curtains and settling in for the evening. But for one small, spiny family at the end of my garden, the day is only just beginning.

Behind my shed, a mother hedgehog has built something rather ingenious: a network of tunnels through a carefully rearranged pile of compost debris, leading into a dome of leaves and vegetation. There are two entrances at the front, and a third at the back that slips under the fence into my neighbour's garden.

If I sit quietly enough as the light fades, I can watch her and her babies emerge, noses first, as they set off on their nightly rounds, snuffling under fences and through flower beds, working their way along the entire run of back gardens on our terrace. Over the course of an evening, they'll check for slugs at Sheila's at number 15, then trundle across the gardens or down the passageway behind the houses to see what's on offer at Deb's at number 41. My neighbours and I feel genuinely lucky to share our gardens with these small, determined travellers.
Watching them, it's easy to forget just how remarkable a journey it is.

The European hedgehog is one of Britain's most recognisable native mammals, found in gardens, hedgerows and green spaces across the country. It's largely insectivorous, and a good night's foraging might yield beetles, caterpillars and earthworms, along with whatever other invertebrates happen to be on the menu. In the process, a hedgehog can cover a surprising amount of ground, sometimes travelling two miles in a single night as it hunts for food and, when the season is right, for a mate. Our garden family, it turns out, is far from unusual in its appetite for exploration.

That need to roam is one of the reasons hedgehogs have become an unlikely barometer for the health of our wider environment. A species that moves between habitats and relies on a broad, varied diet tends to reflect the state of the ecosystem around it. When hedgehog numbers fall, it is often a sign that something bigger is going wrong; when they hold steady or recover, it suggests the landscape is still capable of supporting a rich and connected web of wildlife.
The European hedgehog is now classified as Vulnerable to Extinction in the GB on the Red List for Britain's Mammals.

The State of Britain's Hedgehogs 2022 report found that rural hedgehog populations have declined by somewhere between 30 and 75% since 2000, driven by habitat loss and fragmentation, busier roads, and a shrinking supply of natural food. Genetic isolation, accidental harm and the slow accumulation of toxins in the food chain add further pressure. It's a sobering picture for an animal that has shared our landscapes for thousands of years.

Yet within that same report lies a flicker of hope. While the countryside has struggled with population numbers, hedgehog populations in suburban areas appear to be stabilising. It turns out that our gardens, with their hedges, lawns and untidy corners, may be doing more for hedgehog conservation than we realised, and my own unruly patch behind the shed is proof enough of that for me.

This is where the story becomes something my neighbours and I have witnessed firsthand. Every hedgehog needs to move between gardens in search of food and mates, but modern fencing, with its solid panels and tight-fitting gates, can turn a street of gardens into a row of isolated islands. The solution is refreshingly simple: a "hedgehog highway", just a five-inch gap cut into the base of a fence, is often enough to reconnect a whole neighbourhood's worth of habitat. It's exactly the kind of gap that lets our own hedgehog family pass so freely between the strips of garden from number 15 all the way along to number 41.
There's more you can do too.

Add a shallow dish of water for these warm nights, check for uncovered drains, take care with netting and be mindful of disturbing a pile of garden debris, and a garden can become a true refuge for one of our most vulnerable native species. In a few small steps you can be a hedgehog champion, and if you're curious to learn more, Hedgehog Street has a wealth of information to help and support hedgehogs.

These small, local actions now sit within a much larger vision.  In response to trends highlighted in the State of Britain’s Hedgehogs 2022report, The National Hedgehog Conservation Strategy, developed by the People's Trust for Endangered Species, the British Hedgehog Preservation Society and the IUCN Conservation Planning Specialist Group with input from a range of partners including Natural England, looks ahead to 2053, imagining a Britain where "wild hedgehog populations are thriving from towns to countryside, supported through our combined actions, meeting the needs of people and nature."

Getting there means tackling six priority threats, from habitat loss and vehicle collisions to the everyday hazards hedgehogs face in gardens and on roads, and it means conservationists, government bodies, farmers, developers and householders all pulling in the same direction.

It is a strategy built on the idea that recovery happens at every scale. It includes national monitoring programmes like the People's Trust for Endangered Species national monitoring pilot, initially funded by Natural England Species Recovery Programme (2023–26) and now Heritage Lottery funded.

The programme will improve distribution data to better inform hedgehog recovery and conservation planning and uses citizen science through Mammalweb, enabling enthusiasts to help monitor hedgehogs and wild mammals across the UK; it involves farming incentives such as Countryside Stewardship, the Sustainable Farming Incentive and Biodiversity Net Gain supporting the creation, restoration and connectivity of habitats, including hedgerows and field margins, which are so important for hedgehogs; and it recognises the importance of actions right down to a single gap cut into a garden fence.

Every time I watch our hedgehog family disappear under next door's fence, I'm reminded that this recovery is already happening, one garden at a time. A hedgehog snuffling through the undergrowth on a summer evening is a small sign that a garden, and the wider landscape around it, is still doing its job. With around 5,000 to 7,000 spines to protect it and a lifespan of only two to three years, a hedgehog needs every bit of help it can get.
Fortunately, that help can start with something as small as a gap in a fence.

title: Why light matters: CST’s advice on securing competitive advantage through photonics

content.content: Realising long-term economic growth, national security and resilience from the UK’s strengths in science and technology requires focused support in areas where the UK can secure lasting competitive advantage.

Photonics – the science and application of light – already underpins a broad range of technologies we rely on every day, from fibre optic communications and medical lasers to advanced sensing systems.
It is also a major economic asset. In 2024, the UK photonics sector employed 84,000 people across the UK, contributing £8.6 billion to the economy.
Looking ahead, photonics will play a critical role in emerging fields including optical computing, next generation AI, quantum technologies and advanced manufacturing.

CST member Professor Nick McKeown says: “AI runs on chips that exchange mind-boggling amounts of data to train and run models. Photonic links and chips will shatter the energy and speed barriers holding back the next generation of AI – and the UK has what it takes to lead that revolution."

On 19 February 2026, CST wrote to the Prime Minister, highlighting how the UK’s photonics sector offers a distinctive opportunity to build on existing UK strengths, drive growth and reinforce international leadership.
CST’s recommendations
To help the UK realise this opportunity, CST advised government to take a more coordinated and strategic approach, focusing on three key actions:

As CST member Paul Taylor noted: “Photonics is an underpinning technology, so increasing government support offers an opportunity for growth and global leadership in many important sectors, including defence, clean energy, advanced manufacturing, healthcare and digital infrastructure.”
Working with the sector to build a roadmap

Since publishing this advice, CST and government have engaged closely with the UK photonics sector to support development of a national photonics roadmap, with the aim of better coordinating activities to build on UK strengths.

As part of this, we convened a sector workshop in May 2026, attended by 71 representatives from academia, industry, government departments and investment communities. The session brought together a wide cross-section of the ecosystem – from start-ups and scale-ups to established large enterprises and research organisations – to help identify priorities for growth and leadership.
Three key themes emerged:
Clear opportunities in high-value sectors

Participants highlighted strong near-term high-value opportunities where the UK has credible strengths, particularly in AI infrastructure (e.g. optical interconnects for data centres), defence applications (e.g. such as sensing and secure communications), and advanced manufacturing.

While global competition across the sector is strong, the UK is well placed to compete in high-value niches like specialist components, embedded AI and sensing technologies, by building on existing expertise.
A need for better coordination and shared infrastructure
There was good consensus that improved coordination across the photonics ecosystem will be essential to unlocking growth.

Participants emphasised the importance of access to shared facilities for prototyping, testing and manufacturing – especially for photonic integrated circuits. Improving access to infrastructure, and strengthening links between research, industry and investment, was seen as a very transformative intervention government could make.
Building a stronger UK narrative

Representatives highlighted the need for a clearer, more coherent national story about UK photonics. While photonics supports priorities such as AI, defence and clean energy, participants noted that this breadth can make the sector harder to champion. They therefore emphasised the need to identify where the UK will prioritise its efforts and focus on areas of competitive advantage. A stronger narrative, backed by consistent policy signals and better engagement with industry, would help attract investment and support business scale-up.
Looking ahead
Photonics is already a UK success story, but its future impact depends on effective collaboration between government, industry, and academia.
The development of a national photonics roadmap offers a chance to take a more coordinated approach, which links research excellence with infrastructure, skills and investment.
By acting now, the UK can ensure photonics continues to support economic growth, national security, resilience and technological leadership in the years ahead.

description: Photonics underpins key technologies and UK strengths. CST highlights a clear growth opportunity and calls for coordinated action to build capability and global leadership.

title: Climate adaptation: strengthening the UK’s resilience to climate change

content.content: Climate change is already being felt across the UK, with increasing impacts on people’s lives and the economy. With it now expected that global warming levels will exceed 1.5ºC1 in the next ten years, the need to adapt is urgent.

Ahead of 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30) last November, the Council for Science and Technology (CST) wrote to the Prime Minister making the case for coordinated climate adaptation action.
CST’s recommendations

The Council provided four clear recommendations for government. These focus on measurable targets, better risk monitoring, and clarity about the choices and trade-offs that climate adaptation will require. CST recommended:
You can read CST's recommendations in full here.
Climate resilience panel event

Following this advice, CST led a panel event on 25 February 2026 with the Foundation for Science and Technology (FST). The event brought together scientists, government and wider stakeholders to discuss these recommendations. You can watch the full recording of the event on FST’s website.

Panel members noted that the importance of climate adaptation for the UK’s resilience has long been recognised. Since the UK’s Climate Change Act in 2008, the UK has implemented several adaptation policies and guidance. These include significant investment in flood risk management, reforms to building regulations, commitments to new reservoirs as well as action on water demand and leakage.

However, despite these positive interventions, Professor Jim Hall (Professor of Climate and Environmental Risks at the University of Cambridge and CST member) shared his view that challenges around measuring progress, fragmented responsibilities, and the many competing priorities in government and beyond have led to adaptation slipping down the agenda. This is why CST’s recommendations were developed now and why they are so important.

Professor Mike Tipton (Extreme Environments Lab, University of Portsmouth & President of The Physiological Society) emphasised the importance of the impacts of climate change on the human body. He highlighted that adaptation policies must take account of how the human body responds to environmental stress, such as heat, air pollution, and extreme events. Understanding these physiological limits is essential both for designing effective policies and for engaging the public.

Panellists stressed that adaptation is essential alongside continued action to reduce the carbon emissions that are driving climate change. They reiterated the points made in the CST advice, that clear leadership and coordination from the centre of government are needed to support effective delivery.

Since the event, CST has continued to work with government on implementation of these recommendations, advising on introducing specific and measurable climate adaptation targets and a spatial dashboard to inform policy and spending decisions. CST looks forward to continuing this engagement following the recent publication of the Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment – Independent Assessment (CCRA4-IA).

title: The 2026 National Reference Test: rising attainment in maths and what this means for grades

content.content: The 2026 National Reference Test (NRT) results are out today. They show a long-term trend of slightly improved attainment in GCSE maths, but not in English language. So, to ensure that standards are maintained, we told exam boards to take the results of the NRT into account when setting some grade boundaries in GCSE maths.
What is the National Reference Test?
Every February and March, a sample of year 11 students at more than 330 schools in England sit a short test featuring similar-style questions to those set in GCSE English language and maths exams.
The tests have been running since 2017, when the current GCSE specifications were first examined. That year serves as the benchmark for making comparisons over time.

As it is a consistent test sat each year, it is a highly reliable measure of whether overall attainment in these subjects is going up, down, or staying the same. Where there are genuine changes in the level of attainment over time, the NRT enables us to see it. This extra evidence helps us to maintain standards and ensure that outcomes in GCSE English language and maths reflect any trends in student attainment.
What has the NRT shown and what has Ofqual done?
Maths

The NRT has shown a small rise in attainment in maths at grade 7 in recent years. The trend is now clear and sustained against the 2017 benchmark. It is highly likely that this improvement is also present across the higher grade range. That change is a genuine improvement in what students know, understand and can do.

On this basis we instructed exam boards to reflect this evidence of improvement in their setting of grade boundaries, in the upper grade range. It means those grade boundaries are lower than they otherwise would have been.
English language

In English language, it’s a different picture. Results at grade 7 are not statistically significantly different to 2017. At grade 4, there is an indication that attainment has fallen since 2017. However there has not yet been a consistent enough trend over time to justify any action this year, given the cautious way in which we use evidence from the NRT. As usual we will be looking closely at this again next year, in light of the 2027 NRT results.
What does this mean for students and schools?
The impact on today’s GCSE maths results is a small increase in the number of students achieving higher grades. At grade 4 results are stable as attainment is stable.
Results in English language are stable, with any variation being normal fluctuations we see each year in the proportions of students achieving each grade.
The main takeaway is that the NRT has enabled us to ensure that standards are maintained and rising attainment in GCSE maths has been reflected in students’ results.
You can find more detail about the NRT results in our 2026 NRT annual statement. And for all the data, there’s the National Foundation for Educational Research’s full report.
Michelle Meadows, Chief Standards Adviser, Ofqual

title: Beyond the bite: how science helps the UK stay ahead of mosquito-borne diseases

content.content: For many people, mosquitoes are simply an annoying part of summer. Their familiar buzz is usually the signal to start waving your arms, reach for the insect repellent or wonder where that itchy bite came from.

For scientists, however, that same buzz tells a much bigger story. In the Vector-borne Diseases group at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), we study pathogens that are transmitted by vectors such as mosquitoes. By identifying mosquito species, their locations, and any pathogens they carry, we can better understand how mosquito-borne pathogens move through wildlife populations and whether they pose a disease risk to animals or humans. In other words, while most people are trying to avoid mosquitoes, we are interested in finding them and discovering what viruses they might be carrying.

World Mosquito Day is an opportunity to reflect on how much we have learnt about these tiny vectors and the pathogens they can spread. It also highlights the importance of staying one step ahead of emerging health threats.
Looking for the early warning signs

One of the most important parts of our work is undertaking surveillance of mosquito-borne viruses. We analyse mosquitoes collected from different parts of the country to identify the species present, understand how mosquito populations are changing, and test them for viruses of public and animal health importance, including West Nile virus (WNV), Usutu virus (USUV) and other emerging mosquito-borne viruses.

Alongside mosquito surveillance, we analyse samples from dead wild birds of species known to be susceptible to the viruses of interest. These samples are submitted by APHA regional laboratories, collaborators such as Zoological Society of London (ZSL), and members of the public through initiatives such as Garden Wildlife Health.

People are often surprised to learn that birds are included in routine surveillance. Birds act as hosts for a range of mosquito-borne viruses, allowing them to persist in nature, while mosquitoes transmit the virus between birds, or to animals and humans, where infection may cause disease. By monitoring both, we can build a much clearer picture of how these viruses are circulating in the environment.

We also study how viruses evolve over time by analysing their genetic material, helping us understand where they may have come from and how they are changing. Together, this research helps turn surveillance results into meaningful information that supports future decision-making and government risk assessments.

The value of this work is reflected in recent findings. USUV is an emerging mosquito-borne virus across Europe and is now endemic in southeast England. The virus is classed as a zoonosis, meaning it can cause disease in humans, although this is very rare and so far, no human cases have been recorded in the United Kingdom (UK). However, the virus severely impacts Eurasian Blackbirds (Turdus merula) and in Greater London, Blackbird populations have declined by up to 50% since the virus emerged. Through our surveillance network, USUV was detected in wild birds in Scotland for the first time last year. This finding highlights how important surveillance is, because it shows how rapidly the virus can emerge in new areas and supports the notion that the UK climate is facilitating the emergence and transmission of mosquito-borne viruses.
Finding a virus is only the beginning
Surveillance tells us what is happening in the environment, but additional research is needed to understand why it is happening and what it might mean for animal and human health.

When a virus is detected, our work is just beginning. Once we detect it, we need to answer questions such as: Can native UK mosquitoes transmit it? Which mosquito species are involved in transmission? How quickly can we detect it?

One of the questions we investigate is whether mosquitoes found in the UK can become infected by a virus and be able to transmit it onwards when they feed again. Scientists call this a vector competence study. At the APHA, we have specialist, secure, laboratories where we can investigate if mosquitoes are able to transmit viruses. We work with native UK mosquitoes, but also with exotic, invasive mosquitoes which may inhabit the UK in the future.

To most people, a mosquito is just a mosquito. To us, the differences matter. Different species behave differently, feed on different animals, and vary in how effectively they can transmit viruses. Understanding these differences helps us identify which species may pose the greatest risk and where surveillance efforts should be focused.
Working together through a One Health approach

Mosquito-borne diseases do not respect organisational boundaries. Many of the viruses involved circulate between wildlife, mosquitoes, domestic animals and, sometimes, people. Addressing these threats requires collaboration across sectors, which is why our work follows a One Health approach that recognises that animal, human and environmental health are closely interconnected.

Our research brings together experts from many different fields, including virology, entomology, wildlife health, veterinary science and public health. We work closely with partner organisations across the United Kingdom, such as the United Kingdom Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the ZSL to share knowledge and data, monitor diseases and build a more complete picture of disease risk, so that we are able to respond more effectively if new threats emerge.
Preparing for tomorrow's challenges

The value of surveillance extends beyond the laboratory. The evidence we generate helps inform how the UK prepares for future disease threats and shape policy making. Following the detection of WNV genetic material in mosquito samples from 2023, an updated national contingency plan for WNV has been published. This ensures that, should the situation change, the UK has an up-to-date framework for surveillance, investigation and response.

As our environment continues to change, so will the challenges posed by mosquito-borne diseases. By combining surveillance with laboratory research and working collaboratively across the One Health community, we are building the knowledge needed to protect wildlife, livestock and public health.

This World Mosquito Day, it is worth remembering that behind every mosquito tested and every bird sample analysed is a team of scientists working behind the scenes to protect animal and public health. Our job is not simply to respond to mosquito-borne disease threats, but to stay one step ahead of them.

title: GCSE results day 2026: Everything you need to know including the number grading system

content.content: Thousands of students across the country will soon be finding out their GCSE results and thinking about the next steps in their education.
Here we explain everything you need to know about the big day, from when results day is, to the current 9-1 grading scale, to what your options are if your results aren’t what you’re expecting.
When is GCSE results day 2026?
GCSE results day will be taking place on Thursday the 20 August.
The results will be made available to schools on Wednesday and available to pick up from your school by 8am on Thursday morning.
Schools will issue their own instructions on how and when to collect your results.
When did we change to a number grading scale?
The shift to the numerical grading system was introduced in England in 2017 firstly in English language, English literature, and maths.
By 2020 all subjects were shifted to number grades. This means anyone with GCSE results from 2017-2020 will have a combination of both letters and numbers.

The numerical grading system was to signal more challenging GCSEs and to better differentiate between students’ abilities - particularly at higher grades between the A*-C grades. There only used to be 4 grades between A* and C, now with the numerical grading scale there are 6.
What do the number grades mean?
The grades are ranked from 1, the lowest, to 9, the highest.
The grades don’t exactly translate, but the two grading scales meet at three points as illustrated below.
The bottom of grade 7 is aligned with the bottom of grade A, while the bottom of grade 4 is aligned to the bottom of grade C.
Meanwhile, the bottom of grade 1 is aligned to the bottom of grade G.
What to do if your results weren’t what you were expecting?
If your results weren’t what you were expecting, firstly don’t panic. You have options.
First things first, speak to your school or college – they could be flexible on entry requirements if you’ve just missed your grades.
They’ll also be able to give you the best tailored advice on whether re-sitting while studying for your next qualifications is a possibility.
Resits
If you’re really unhappy with your results you can enter to resit all GCSE subjects in summer 2026. You can also take autumn exams in GCSE English language and maths.
Speak to your sixth form or college to decide when it’s the best time for you to resit a GCSE exam.
Look for other courses with different grade requirements
Entry requirements vary depending on the college and course. Ask your school for advice, and call your college or another one in your area to see if there’s a space on a course you’re interested in.
Consider V Levels and T Levels

If you're weighing up your next steps, you'll have more routes to choose from than ever. Alongside A levels, you can opt for T Levels, which combine classroom learning with substantial workplace experience, or a fully-funded apprenticeship if you're under 25.

From next year, V Levels will also be introduced, sitting alongside expanded T Levels as a new technical pathway. There's no wrong door, only different routes that suit your individual ambitions, so it's worth exploring what each option involves before deciding what's right for you.
Consider an apprenticeship
Apprenticeships combine a practical training job with study too. They’re open to you if you’re 16 or over, living in England, and not in full time education.
As an apprentice you’ll be a paid employee, have the opportunity to work alongside experienced staff, gain job-specific skills, and get time set aside for training and study related to your role.
You can find out more about how to apply here.
Talk to a National Careers Service (NCS) adviser
The National Career Service is a free resource that can help you with your career planning. Give them a call to discuss potential routes into higher education, further education, or the workplace.

Whatever your results, if you want to find out more about all your education and training options, as well as get practical advice about your exam results, visit the National Careers Service page and Skills for Careers to explore your study and work choices.

title: Putting Nature at the Heart of Healthcare: My Reflections from Bristol

content.content: By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England

In this blog, NE's Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her recent visit to healthcare sites in Bristol to explore how partners are incorporating nature into health and wellbeing, and discusses Natural England's role in this.

One of the moments that stayed with me from my visit to Bristol was sitting in the greenhouse in the community allotment at Southmead Hospital and hearing how this green space on a busy hospital estate has become a place of calm, connection and recovery for patients, staff and local people.
It was a powerful reminder that nature is not a nice-to-have in healthcare. It is part of what helps people feel well, recover well and live well.

Across my day in Bristol, I saw how partners are bringing nature and health closer together from a specialist mental health ward, to a community-focused GP practice, to one of the country’s largest hospital estates.

For too long, nature and health have often been treated as separate issues. But the evidence, and the lived experience of communities across England, tell us something different. Access to nature supports our physical health, our mental wellbeing and our quality of life. In fact, 90% of adults in England say green and natural spaces are good for their mental health and wellbeing.
That is why Natural England’s new strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, champions creating healthier places for people to live, work and spend time.
Nature is part of our health infrastructure

When we think about healthcare, we naturally think about hospitals, GP surgeries, medicines and treatments. All of those are vital. But we also need to recognise the role nature plays in supporting health and wellbeing long before people need clinical care.

A walk in a local park, access to a community garden, or time spent in a wildlife-rich green space can all make a positive difference to people's lives. Yet access to nature is not experienced equally. One in five households do not have access to a green or blue space within a 15-minute walk, with the greatest inequalities often affecting more deprived communities.

At Natural England, we want everyone to have the opportunity to access and benefit from nature, whatever their postcode. We also know that healthy natural environments can strengthen communities, support economic growth and build resilience to climate change. That is why investment in nature should be seen as investment in healthy places and people.
Seeing what's possible
What I saw in Bristol showed how this ambition can be translated into practical action.

At Blackberry Hill Hospital, Avon and Wiltshire Mental Health Partnership NHS Trust has incorporated nature into the design and operation of the new Kingfisher Ward, recognising the role that nature-rich environments can play in supporting recovery and wellbeing.

At Charlotte Keel Medical Centre, partners including Alive Activities and the West of England Mayoral Combined Authority have helped transform an outdoor courtyard space, demonstrating how even busy urban healthcare settings can create opportunities for connecting with nature. Over lunch they described to me what a difference it makes to the quality of breaks at work for staff, and how the courtyard garden has supported patients, some of whom now volunteer their time to look after the space.

And at Southmead Hospital, North Bristol NHS Trust is showing how a major healthcare estate can work harder for both people and Nature through community allotments, green infrastructure and biodiversity improvements that support health, wellbeing and environmental outcomes.
Each project was different, but the message was consistent: when organisations work together, nature can become part of everyday care, not an optional extra.

What impressed me most was the strength of the partnerships behind this work. Across Bristol, NHS organisations, local government, public health teams, community groups and environmental organisations are collaborating around a shared vision. Through initiatives such as green social prescribing, nature-based health projects and wider place-based partnerships, they are demonstrating how health and nature objectives can reinforce one another.
Better outcomes for people and nature
What gives me optimism is that this is not a choice between helping people or helping nature. The most successful examples deliver both.

Creating greener places can improve wellbeing, support biodiversity, strengthen community resilience and help us adapt to climate change at the same time. These are not competing goals. They are mutually reinforcing.

Research suggests that regular access to greenspace could reduce GP visits by 28% and save the NHS an estimated £2.1 billion each year. At a time when health services are under increasing pressure, this is a powerful reminder that prevention matters just as much as treatment.

To support organisations looking to take practical action, Natural England has worked with NHS England and the Centre for Sustainable Healthcare to develop the Nature for Health Resource Hub, bringing together tools, guidance and case studies that help healthcare sites improve their green spaces.
The people I met in Bristol are showing what that looks like in practice, with commitment, imagination and care. There is much we can learn from them.
Our commitment
Natural England's ambition is clear: we want nature to be part of everyday life for everyone.

That means restoring nature, improving access to green and blue spaces, and working with partners across the health, planning, environmental and local government sectors to tackle inequalities and improve wellbeing.
The examples I saw in Bristol show what is possible. The challenge now is to build on these successes and make them the norm rather than the exception.

title: Designing GOV.UK Chat for the GOV.UK app
authors: Christine Wuerth, Lead Designer, GOV.UK Chat

content.content: GOV.UK Chat is an experimental AI tool that can help users get quick answers from government content. Our first scaled tests began with a web-based pilot in 2024. Since then we’ve learned much about designing accessible and transparent chat interfaces. The GOV.UK app provided an opportunity to test and refine GOV.UK Chat in a mobile environment. It’s part of the personalised experience of government that GDS is building in the app, as set out in the Roadmap for Modern Digital Government.
In this post, we share what we learned adapting GOV.UK Chat for the GOV.UK app and how user research shaped the design.
Designing for the GOV.UK app

Creating an AI-powered conversational experience was new territory for us when we started working on GOV.UK Chat almost two years ago. Designing for a live, conversation-based interaction with a generative AI system is very different to other things we design at GDS and requires different skills.

While starting with insights from the web, the new context of the app meant there was plenty for us to learn and adjust, including using native interaction patterns and creating new ones. A series of user research rounds and a small-scale test phase in the app enabled us to iterate our designs based on app-specific evidence.
Designing for smaller screens

Because mobile screens are smaller, we needed to use space more carefully. The screen space is more limited, so we tweaked elements to make better use of it. For example, the experience on the web included a set of three introductory messages telling users about the technology used, and the potential inaccuracy of AI-generated answers. For the app experience, we managed to condense the content to fit into one message without losing clarity.

We removed the chat avatar from the chatbot messages to save space and instead used colour and contrast to clearly distinguish between GOV.UK Chat messages and user messages. To match the app colour system, we also created a light and dark mode, using the new brand colour palette.

We also needed to address new accessibility challenges. For example, we needed to ensure elements like the input field still worked well when people increased text size on their phones. We also ensured screen readers such as VoiceOver and TalkBack announce the character limit for the text input (if enabled in accessibility settings).
Intuitive user interface

We wanted to make the GOV.UK Chat app experience feel familiar and smooth. Shifting to the app, we needed to adapt designs to use app-specific design patterns, and to work natively and intuitively across both iOS and Android.

Beyond that, we made small user interface (UI) adjustments like rounding the corners of chat bubbles, and carefully considered micro-interactions like how messages appear, how elements transition between states (for example, the send button), and how to clearly signal when a response is being generated through a loading state. We grounded the design in established conversational interface patterns. Where it was appropriate, we incorporated thoughtful additions to make the experience feel distinctively GOV.UK, while remaining intuitive.
A new way to interact with government
A conversational, AI-powered way to interact with government is also new for our users, requiring us to explain what to expect through a 3-screen onboarding experience.
Based on user insights, we reduced this down to three main messages, one per screen:

We want to be clear with users about what Chat can and cannot do and be upfront about the small, unavoidable risk of inaccuracy with AI tools. Our aim with the design is to set appropriate expectations, and provide an easy way to verify answers with links to the source guidance of every answer.
Making GOV.UK Chat distinct but not different
We also needed to apply the new GOV.UK brand. As an experimental, AI-powered feature, we wanted it to be distinct but sit comfortably and recognisably within the GOV.UK brand.

We also needed the look and feel to set the right expectations. GOV.UK Chat currently focuses on getting quick answers based exclusively on GOV.UK guidance. Feedback from users told us the experience felt more capable than they had expected from a government chatbot. Our aim was to not over-state what GOV.UK Chat can do today, while allowing flexibility to grow with future capabilities.
What’s next

There are still many things we want to improve. Now that GOV.UK Chat is available to app users, we can increase our understanding of real interactions and continue to make evidence-based improvements. Research continues to identify opportunities to improve the experience, and we're prioritising those improvements in future releases. First up, we are working on helping users ask their first question, especially for those with little to no AI experience. As more people use GOV.UK Chat in the app, we will continue learning from real-world interactions and improving the experience based on evidence.
